newsitem.title: USA: How much medical data on politicians is enough?. [CORRECTED 19:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: How much medical data on politicians is enough?. [CORRECTED 19:40 GMT]

text.p: Bill Clinton and Bob Dole have given voters extensive details about their medical histories, and some experts warn that too much openness could be harmful to the health of political leaders. (Corrects to make clear that sources cited are experts on the subject but not doctors.)
The motives behind the disclosure by the two election rivals are sharply different. One wants to show he is not too old for the job. The other is trying to stop unfounded rumours.

When Republican Dole turned 73 in July, he sought to calm voter doubts about his age by releasing a detailed summary of his health records -- with his chief physician publicly saying he was in excellent health.

The White House had issued a standard written statement in the spring following Clinton's annual physical at Bethesda Naval Hospital, so officials saw no need for the 50-year-old Democratic incumbent to match's Dole's declaration.

They were wrong. Talk radio shows and internet chat rooms turned into rumour mills that Clinton was afflicted with everything from heart problems to venereal disease. It was clear the situation was festering out of control when White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry, fielding reporters questions last week about Clinton's health, was bluntly asked: "Does he have a sexually transmitted disease?"

In an unusual move for an incumbent president, the White House put out a detailed summary of Clinton's medical history in which his physician declared he has "no history of hypertension, diabetes, tuberculosis, sexually transmitted disease, cancer, stroke or heart disease."
So we now know Dole weighs 178 pounds to Clinton's 216, that both men have normal cholesterol -- 154 for Dole and 191 for Clinton -- and that Dole's blood pressure is 100/60 to Clinton's 126/70.
The White House also said Clinton underwent a test for HIV, the virus that causes AIDS, in 1990 and it was negative. The test was said to be part of an insurance physical.
McCurry said the medical history was as "complete as it gets" and should lay questions about Clinton's health to rest "once and for all."

Dole, in an interview with ABC's "Good Morning America" that was broadcast on Monday, did not seem satisfied. "Why did he wait? Why did it take so long?" he asked. "It seems to me that with the problems we've had in the past with some candidates, we ought to give people the information."

But how much information is enough? Some experts argue for full disclosure because presidential health secrets have been kept from the public in the past. Others say some things should remain private.

Woodrow Wilson suffered a massive stroke in 1919 but his wife and aides ran the country without disclosing how bad his condition was. In 1956 Dwight Eisenhower had a heart attack that was disclosed -- along with a doctor's observation that he "had a good bowel movement."

"Full disclosure of medical history serves the public well and ultimately it serves the politician well," said Stephen Bloom of the University of Iowa, who has done extensive research into presidential health coverups.

"I want to know as much as I can about the person who will be elected president," said Bloom, an associate journalism professor. "This is one puzzle piece that should be controlled by voters, not by politicians. It is fundamental information."
But George Annas of Boston University said even presidents have a right to privacy. "Presidents have always been more likely to be killed or disabled by assassins than by diseases," he said.

"We are rapidly approaching the point of diminishing returns" when it comes to medical disclosure, he wrote in the New England Journal of Medicine. "Unless we want to discourage our presidents ... and possible presidential candidates from seeking medical assistance in times of physical and psychological distress, we must show at least some respect for their medical privacy."

Annas and others who question full disclosure note that "the only U.S. president who actually died of a pre-existing condition that made his death in office likely was Franklin Roosevelt," who passed away soon after he began an unprecedented fourth term.
Roosevelt was confined to a wheelchair during his presidency after he was stricken with polio as an adult. He died of congestive heart disease.
Bloom, however, argues that "in a political system like ours, we need to know as much as we can about the people who will be ultimately running the city, the state or the nation."
"Its ironic that if you serve in the military, you have to take an HIV test, but if you are commander-in-chief of the military, you don't."
